title: Shortness of breath in a 68-year-old (ED)

patient.name: Harold Bennett
patient.chiefComplaint: Worsening shortness of breath for two weeks
patient.setting: Emergency department, sitting upright on a stretcher

persona.affect: Tired, a little breathless, polite, worried but trying to make light of it
persona.speakingStyle: Short sentences; pauses to catch his breath after longer answers; plain everyday words, no medical jargon
persona.worries: Worried he will be admitted and miss his granddaughter’s birthday this weekend; quietly worried it is his heart again
persona.background: Retired city bus driver, married, enjoys fishing and his grandchildren

doorSign.task: Mr. Bennett, 68, presents with two weeks of worsening shortness of breath. Take a focused history, perform a focused cardiovascular and respiratory examination, then present your summary, differential diagnosis and initial plan.

doorInstructions.task: Take a focused history and perform a focused physical examination. Share your impressions with the patient before you leave. You will then write a post-encounter note.

history.openingStatement: I just can’t catch my breath. It’s been getting worse for a couple of weeks.

facts.answer: It came on gradually about two weeks ago and has got steadily worse. The last three days have been the worst.

general_appearance.default: Older man sitting bolt upright, mildly breathless at rest, pausing mid-sentence to breathe; alert and oriented; looks tired.

pulse_radial.default: Radial pulse {vitals.hr} beats/min, regular rhythm, low volume.

jvp_inspection.default: JVP clearly elevated: venous column about 9 cm above the sternal angle at 30° (estimated RAP ~14 cmH2O), pulsating up to the angle of the jaw.

hepatojugular_reflux.default: Positive: with sustained right upper quadrant pressure the JVP rises about 4 cm and stays up while pressure is held.

precordial_inspection.default: Apical impulse visible lateral to the midclavicular line; no scars or deformity.

pmi_palpation.cardiac_mitral: PMI displaced laterally to the 6th intercostal space at the anterior axillary line; diffuse (about 4 cm).

cardiac_mitral.text: Tachycardic, regular. Soft grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating toward the axilla. A low-pitched extra sound after S2 is faintly audible.

default.text: Tachycardic, regular rhythm; normal S1 and S2; no murmur at this area.

cardiac_mitral.text: Low-pitched S3 gallop at the apex, loudest with the patient rolled onto the left side.

left_lateral_decubitus.text: Loud low-pitched S3 gallop at the apex — clearest with the patient rolled onto the left side.

cardiac_tricuspid.text: Faint low-pitched extra sound after S2, better heard at the apex.

expectedDifferential.diagnosis: Acute decompensated heart failure (HFrEF, ischaemic cardiomyopathy)
expectedDifferential.rationale: Known EF ~30% after MI; orthopnea, PND, weight gain, bilateral pitting edema, raised JVP, positive HJR, displaced PMI, S3, bibasal crackles and right effusion. Precipitants: stopped furosemide, dietary salt load, recent NSAID.

expectedDifferential.diagnosis: Acute coronary syndrome as a precipitant
expectedDifferential.rationale: Prior MI and multiple risk factors; must be excluded with ECG and troponin even without chest pain (silent ischaemia in diabetes).
Crackles and hypoxia, but afebrile, dry cough and bilateral findings with edema argue against.
Tachycardia and hypoxia; less likely given symmetric edema, gradual course and clear volume overload.
30 pack-year history, but no wheeze or sputum and clear signs of fluid overload.

expectedDifferential.diagnosis: Other causes of fluid overload (renal failure, cirrhosis)
expectedDifferential.rationale: Consider with labs; cardiac signs make these less likely.

Increasingly breathless on exertion over the past fortnight.

Breathlessness when lying down, slept in a recliner.

Bilateral leg swelling with recent weight gain.

Stopped his water pill and ate a salty diet recently.

differential.rationale: Known reduced EF with orthopnea, PND, weight gain, raised JVP, S3, crackles and edema; stopped diuretic and salt load.
Prior MI and risk factors; must be excluded as a precipitant even without chest pain.
Crackles and cough, though afebrile with bilateral findings and edema.
